lesson.title: The Fairest Draw: Simple Random Samples
lesson.summary: A simple random sample gives every possible group of a given size from the population an equal chance of being chosen, making it the benchmark against which every other sampling method is judged.
lesson.body:
A simple random sample, almost always abbreviated SRS, of size n is a sample chosen in such a way that every possible group of n individuals from the population has an equal chance of being the one selected. This definition is slightly stronger than simply saying every individual has an equal chance of being picked; it requires that every possible combination of n individuals be equally likely, which rules out certain sampling methods that treat individuals fairly one at a time but still favor certain combinations of individuals over others.

Walk through how an SRS is actually carried out. Suppose a teacher wants to select an SRS of 5 students from a class roster of 25 students to interview about the course. She first lists all 25 students and assigns each one a unique two digit label, 01 through 25. Then, using a table of random digits or a random number generator, she reads off two digit numbers, ignoring any number above 25 and ignoring any repeat of a number already chosen, until she has collected 5 distinct labels, say 03, 11, 14, 19, and 22. The students holding those five labels form the simple random sample. Because the digit-reading process treats every two digit number from 01 to 25 identically, every one of the many possible groups of 5 students out of 25 had an equal chance of being the group actually chosen.

The SRS matters so much in this course because it is the foundation on which the formulas for standard error, margin of error, and confidence intervals are built; those formulas assume that the sample behaves like an SRS, meaning its randomness is not distorted by favoring certain individuals or certain combinations of individuals over others. When a sample departs from being an SRS, for example because it was collected through convenience or voluntary response, the mathematical guarantees behind those formulas no longer strictly apply, even if the arithmetic can still technically be computed.

It is worth contrasting an SRS with a method that sounds similar but is not equivalent: systematic sampling, where a researcher picks every tenth name from an alphabetized list starting at a random point. That method does give every individual an equal chance of selection, but it does not give every possible group of n individuals an equal chance, since, for instance, two people whose names are next to each other alphabetically could never both end up in the same systematic sample. This distinction is exactly why the definition of an SRS specifically requires equally likely groups, not merely equally likely individuals.

An SRS is also the building block that other, more elaborate designs are built on top of. Stratified random sampling, covered next, works by first splitting a population into subgroups and then drawing an SRS from within each subgroup separately, which shows how the core machinery of the SRS, equal chance selection through a random number generator, gets reused as a component inside more sophisticated sampling plans rather than being replaced by them.
